chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that he said:

Regarding a man who gives charity (sadaqah) to his children who have reached maturity, if they do not take possession of it until he dies, it is considered inheritance. And if he gives charity to those who have not reached maturity from his children, it is valid, because their father is the one who manages their affairs.
And he said: 'One does not return (revoke) the charity if one seeks the Countenance of Allah, Exalted and Glorious.'

And he said: 'The gift (hibah) and the grant (nihlah), one returns in it if one wishes, whether it was taken possession of or not, except for the close relative (of the donor), for indeed he does not return in it.'

key_terms.صَدَقَة: Charity, a voluntary gift often considered irrevocable if for God's sake
key_terms.نِحْلَة: Grant or endowment, a type of gift
key_terms.هِبَة: Gift, a transfer of ownership that is generally revocable

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between sadaqah and hibah in Shia jurisprudence regarding children?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Baqir, highlighting the critical Shia legal distinction between sadaqah (charity) and hibah (gift) based on the child's maturity and actual possession (qabd). The Imam clarifies that while gifts to minors are irrevocable due to the father's guardianship, adult children's charity remains part of the estate until possession is complete, whereas general gifts are revocable unless given to a close relative (dhil rahm), reflecting the principle of 'not returning charity if sought for God's countenance.'
